title: Sebastian and the Weather
premise: Rafael Vasquez has written postcards for five years to the burned house of his childhood — letters addressed to his mother, who may or may not be alive, in a language the family abandoned to survive. At his father's funeral, a stranger calls the family by their pre-exile name, Solano, and reveals that the mother sent one final letter before the fire, a sentence Rafael has spent his life refusing to translate. As he traces the stranger through a coastal town that remembers too much, Rafael learns the fire was no accident, that his father chose the new name to bury a betrayal, and that the untranslatable sentence is a confession of what his mother did to keep them alive. In the end, Rafael writes the sentence out in full for the first time, mails it to the burned address anyway, and finally signs it with both names.
about_author: Oscar Blackwood is the pen name of a former court translator who spent a decade rendering testimony for families torn between two languages. He writes literary fiction about the silences immigrants carry, and lives within sight of a coastline he refuses to name.

chapters.title: Postcards to a Burned House
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. On the morning of his father's funeral, Rafael writes his 1,826th postcard to an address that no longer exists, revealing his five-year ritual of almost-saying. The emotional beat is quiet compulsion — devotion disguised as habit, and the reader learns he has never once finished a sentence.

chapters.title: The Man Who Said Solano
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. At the funeral, a gaunt stranger named Ilya approaches the coffin and calls the family Solano — a name Rafael has never heard. His aunt visibly flinches and hustles Ilya out. The beat is destabilization: Rafael's entire identity tilts on one spoken word.

chapters.title: What the Aunt Burned Twice
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, with a flashback to childhood. Rafael confronts his aunt Dolores, who admits the family name was changed after 'the fire' but refuses to say what burned besides the house. He finds a scorched corner of an old photograph. The beat is the first crack in the family's protective silence.

chapters.title: A Stranger's Debt
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Ilya reveals he knew Rafael's mother in the old country and that she entrusted him with a sealed letter to deliver 'when Rafael is ready.' He has carried it for twenty years, waiting. The beat is dread wrapped in tenderness — the letter exists, but Ilya won't hand it over yet.

chapters.title: The Language We Didn't Teach You
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Rafael realizes the postcards he's written for five years are in his mother's abandoned mother tongue — words he never learned, arriving from somewhere he can't explain. He visits the burned lot and finds the foundation stones. The beat is uncanny inheritance: language outliving its speakers.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Grave
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Rafael discovers his father's grave is registered under Solano — the father secretly reclaimed the old name before dying. Dolores confesses the name was changed to hide that the mother informed on neighbors to buy the family's escape. The beat is horror at the price of survival.

chapters.title: The Fire Was a Signature
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Ilya admits he set the fire — at the mother's own request — to destroy the evidence of her betrayal before the family could be traced by it. The mother stayed behind and died in the house she chose to burn. The beat is devastating reversal: the fire was an act of love.

chapters.title: Ready
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Ilya, now dying himself, finally gives Rafael the sealed letter. Rafael recognizes his mother's handwriting and the single unfinished sentence — the same one his postcards have been circling for five years. The beat is confrontation with the object of a lifetime's avoidance.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, interior and close. Rafael sits with the letter through one long night, attempting translation after translation, each failing. He finally understands the sentence isn't a confession or an apology — it's a request to be remembered by the name she betrayed. The beat is the climax: acceptance without absolution.

chapters.title: Signed, Both Names
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, epilogue-like. Rafael writes his first completed letter — the sentence translated in full — mails it to the burned address, and carves 'Solano' beside his father's name on the grave. He signs his own postcards with both names for the first time. The beat is resolution: identity as something carried, not chosen.
